Short-haul carriers will experience three types of adverse effects. First, some truckload traffic will be diverted by the ability of long-haul carriers to provide more single-line service. Secondly, they will lose protection from competition on those portions of their service routes encompassed by the expanded zones. Thirdly, in many cases the pecuniary value attached of their operating certificates will be substantially diminished. Undoubtedly, these effects will curtail revenues in the short-term. These effects may linger in the long-term for many firms, which do not or cannot adjust their operations to the changes caused by our revised regulations. Nevertheless, we believe the overall benefits to the public of more singleline service and greater flexibility of local operations within urban areas amply justifies our actions in this 68 Short-haul carriers should also receive some proceeding. benefit from the expansion of service areas effectuated by the new rules. Finally, we believe that many of the fears of increased competition expressed by these carriers are exaggerated for they are already established operations possessing much experience and expertise. As noted in the Interim Report, since local operations within commercial zones are totally exempt from our economic regulation, short-haul carriers will not be forced to adhere to published tariff schedules when operating within exempt areas.
